_comment: Demo research documents, media items and one extra course. Documents that point at genuinely public sources (India Code, NALSA, the RTI portal) use their real URLs, because those are real and useful; anything that would be a fabricated record uses a demo URL with a title saying so.

documents.title: DEMO: Recall provisions in comparative practice
documents.summary: DEMO DOCUMENT - sample content. A survey of recall mechanisms in other jurisdictions: thresholds, minimum periods after election, who verifies signatures, and what has actually happened where recall exists. Written to inform the safeguards a workable Indian law would need.

documents.title: DEMO: State laws providing recall at panchayat and municipal level
documents.summary: DEMO DOCUMENT - sample content. Which states already allow the recall of local representatives, what the thresholds are, how often it has been used, and what happened. This is the strongest evidence that recall is not alien to Indian law.

documents.title: DEMO: How we calculate and check attendance figures
documents.summary: DEMO DOCUMENT - sample content. The method behind every attendance percentage on this site: which register is used, how partial terms are handled, why a member who joined mid-session is not compared with one who did not, and what the figure does not tell you.

documents.title: DEMO: Written submission to the Maharashtra committee

documents.title: DEMO: Article 326 poster

course.title: Using the RTI Act to hold an office to account
course.title_hi: किसी कार्यालय को जवाबदेह ठहराने के लिए आरटीआई अधिनियम का उपयोग
course.summary: A practical course on the Right to Information Act: what it covers, how to word a request that gets answered, the deadlines, and what to do when they are missed.

lessons.title: What the Act actually covers
lessons.body:
DEMO LESSON - sample content.

The Right to Information Act, 2005 gives you access to information HELD BY a public authority IN MATERIAL FORM. Those two conditions do most of the work.

'Held by' means the office that actually has the record, which is often not the department at the top. If you send your application to the wrong office, Section 6(3) requires them to transfer it within five days - but that costs you five days, so it is worth getting right.

'In material form' is the condition people trip over. The Act gives you documents, files, notings, emails, contracts, reports, samples and models. It does not require anyone to compose an answer for you. 'Provide a copy of the sanction order for the road work in ward 12' is a valid request. 'Why has the road in ward 12 not been repaired?' is not, and gives the office an easy refusal.

The practical translation: ask yourself which document would contain the answer, and ask for that document.

Section 6(2) is worth knowing too. You do not have to give any reason for wanting the information, and you cannot be asked for one. If an official asks why you want it, they are wrong, and you can say so.

lessons.title: Wording it, and filing it
lessons.body:
DEMO LESSON - sample content.

Number your questions. An application with five numbered points gets a reply addressing five numbered points; an application written as a paragraph gets a paragraph that answers whichever part was easiest.

Narrow the period. 'All correspondence relating to water supply' invites a refusal on the grounds that it would disproportionately divert resources. '1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025' does not.

Ask for the form you want. Certified copies are usually more useful than inspection, and you are entitled to ask.

The fee is ten rupees for a central public authority, by Indian Postal Order, demand draft, banker's cheque or court fee stamp. States set their own, so check your state's RTI Rules. If you hold a BPL card you pay nothing under Section 7(5) - attach a copy.

Keep three things: a photocopy of the application, the postal receipt, and the date of despatch. Every deadline that follows is counted from that date, so if you lose it you have lost your ability to appeal on time.

One last line worth adding to every application: ask them to tell you the name and designation of the First Appellate Authority for that office. You will need it if they do not reply, and asking now saves you a fortnight later.

lessons.title: The deadlines, and what to do when they pass
lessons.body:
DEMO LESSON - sample content.

Thirty days for a reply. Forty-eight hours if the information concerns the life or liberty of a person. Thirty-five days if you filed through an Assistant PIO.

If they miss the deadline, Section 7(6) entitles you to the information free of any further fee. Say so in your appeal - it is frequently ignored.

A refusal must name the specific clause of Section 8 or 9 relied on. 'Exempt under Section 8' with no clause is not a lawful refusal, and saying so in the first appeal usually resolves it. Section 10 also requires partial disclosure: if part of a record is exempt, the rest must still be given.

First appeal: within 30 days, no fee, to the First Appellate Authority in the same office - an officer senior to the PIO. They must decide within 30 days, or 45 with reasons recorded.

Second appeal: within 90 days, no fee, to the Central Information Commission for central authorities or your State Information Commission. The Commission can order disclosure and impose a penalty on a PIO who refused without reasonable cause.

Attach everything at each stage - the original application, the proof of despatch, and any reply. A second appeal without them is usually returned, and you will have lost months.

lessons.title: Using what comes back
lessons.body:
DEMO LESSON - sample content.

An RTI reply is a primary public record. That makes it one of the strongest things you can attach to anything else you do.

On this platform, an RTI reply can be cited as the source for a citizen report card, attached to a correction about a representative's record, or added to the Research Centre so the next person does not have to file the same request.

It is also the standard follow-up to a representation. If you wrote to your MP or MLA and heard nothing, an RTI to the concerned department asking 'what action was taken on representation dated X' creates a record of the silence itself. That record is often more useful than the original answer would have been.

And if the reply shows something is genuinely wrong, you now have documented evidence rather than an impression - which is what any court, committee or journalist will ask you for first.

questions.q: Which of these is a valid RTI request?
options: Provide a copy of the sanction order for the road work in ward 12
Why has the road in ward 12 not been repaired?
Explain the department's policy on road repairs
Do you think the road work was handled properly?
questions.explanation: The Act gives you access to information held in material form. Ask for the RECORD that would contain the answer, not for an explanation or an opinion - the last three all invite a refusal on the grounds that no such information is held.

questions.q: How long does a public authority normally have to reply?
options: 30 days
7 days
60 days
90 days
questions.explanation: 30 days normally, 48 hours where the information concerns the life or liberty of a person, and 35 days if the application was filed through an Assistant PIO.

questions.q: You get no reply at all within the time limit. What are you entitled to?
options: The information free of any further fee, under Section 7(6)
Nothing until you file a second appeal
Compensation from the department
An automatic escalation to the Information Commission
questions.explanation: Section 7(6) means a missed deadline entitles you to the information without further fee. It is worth quoting in your first appeal, because it is frequently overlooked.

questions.q: Do you have to explain why you want the information?
options: No - Section 6(2) says you cannot even be asked
Yes, on the application form
Only for information about public officials
Only if the authority requests it
questions.explanation: Section 6(2) is explicit: no reason is required and none may be demanded. If an official asks, they are wrong.

questions.q: A refusal says only 'exempt under Section 8'. Is that lawful?
options: No - it must name the specific clause relied on
Yes, Section 8 is sufficient on its own
Yes, but only for central authorities
It depends on the fee paid
questions.explanation: A refusal has to identify the specific clause. Section 10 also requires partial disclosure, so even where part of a record is genuinely exempt, the remainder must still be provided.

questions.q: How long do you have to file a first appeal, and what does it cost?
options: 30 days, no fee
90 days, no fee
30 days, ten rupees
There is no first appeal - you go straight to the Commission
questions.explanation: First appeal: within 30 days of the decision or of the date it was due, no fee, to the First Appellate Authority in the same office. The second appeal is 90 days, also free, and goes to the Information Commission.
